utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom. And good afternoon, Mr. Sladojevic, again. The witness should be brought in, please. We go into closed session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Good afternoon, sir. Welcome back to the courtroom. I have to remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth still applies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Sladojevic is with us, and I think there's no need to give you the guidance again. Mr. Tolimir, please continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I wish peace onto this house. I wish that this court day finish in keeping with God's will. I greet the witness, General Savcic, and his lawyer, and everyone present in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us begin where we left off yesterday. Yesterday we looked at P125.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I please call it up in e-court so we can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And, please, Mr. Savcic, let us make a pause between questions and answer, and speak more slowly, because we want every word to be interpreted and recorded on LiveNote. This is the paper that has been shown to you before, and yesterday you answered a couple of questions about it. My question is: When you just take a glance at the paper on the left, can you tell us if this has been processed by a teletype and if it bears any trace of teletype processing?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On this paper, you can't see any of that. There is no imprint of the teletype machine. There is no trace that the document has ever gone through a teletype.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see 1D744, page 40, in Serbian; page 27 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Before that, let us say that this is a statement you have given to the OTP.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked for 27 in English and 40 in Serbian, lines 32 to 34. It's the first two -- it's the first few lines in English. Thank you, Aleksander.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please, in the course of the examination-in-chief, in Banja Luka, on the 17th of October, did you let the Prosecutor know, and did you state, that the problem with this paper is that it had not been processed by a teletype?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Among other things, I drew their attention to that fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see page 40, lines 18 to 21. On page 41 in Serbian, and that's still page 27 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Before that, let me ask you: When did you give this interview to the Prosecution in Banja Luka? Because only the date is indicated, not the year.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the extent I remember, I think it's 2005, but I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We have now moved from the page where you discussed the document to the following page, where the investigator tells you these teletype documents never bear a signature below. That's line 7 in English. And you say, I quote, well, that's precisely the point that this is not a teletyped document. If it were, there would be no problem. "I," and then something unclear, "... am not denying. I don't know. I can't remember." But this issue is really questionable. It's printed by a typewriter, on a typewriter. I mean, if it were teletype, this signature would be here, and that's important. You see, it's a big difference. As for the contents, if it were my document, I really cannot confirm now that it was me, because, look, it says here, I practically - and I don't know why I would be doing that - am conveying something General Tolimir is suggesting. It says clearly: "Assistant commander of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska for security intelligence affairs, hereby proposes the following measures." Since you then indicated that this was not a teletype document and that it does not conform to the rules of official correspondence, tell us, please, if a document like this had been processed, would it have had to be recorded, would it have to bear the traces of teletype processing on a perforated sheet, and would the typing be in the lettering that is specific to a teletype machine?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. The fonts, the -- the lettering on the teleprinter, is different from the typing on a typewriter. They do not have the diacritics that are typical of the Serbian and some other languages, so you can clearly see the difference between something that is teletyped and something that is written on a typewriter, even if we are to disregard the differences in the type of paper, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, did General Tolimir, from wherever he was, have the possibility of tele -- the possibility of sending a telegram? Would he need a teletype, and would he need your help to send a communication?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know perfectly well that I had no such means of communication. And even if you had asked me to help you out with that, I would have been unable to. For communications, we mostly used hand-held radios and mobile radios, and those are mainly short-wave devices where we could increase the range through a repeater. But those were radio communications. We had no other equipment, especially not equipment for sending telegrams. Except in the duty service of the military police in Nova Kasaba; they had such machine. In Crna Rijeka, we used the communications of the Main Staff and through them we received -- we received those communications and then the encrypting officer would bring it to us, it was a distance of a couple of hundred metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: For clarification, oh, it was just corrected. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon to you and Your Honours. Mr. President, with all due respect, I've listened to the witness's answer in relation to the question. I can see that it is not responsive to General Tolimir's question which concerned his -- General Tolimir's ability to communicate from "wherever he was." With respect to that question, I would object to it because it's -- it's not sufficiently clear where he was, in order for the witness to properly be able to answer that. And if General Tolimir would like an answer to that question, I would ask him to phrase it in a manner and identify where he was, when he was at that location, so that the witness can answer intelligently whether or not he had the ability to communicate, as he has put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, a clear question is the best way to get a clear response. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: General, since the Prosecutor wants to know where I was, my question is: From the place called Borike where we spent the night along with the others, was it possible to send a telegram through the Rogatica Brigade to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the broader area of Borike, perhaps not, but somewhere there, there was this vehicle of theirs that we were able to use.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us, if I was able to write a telegram in longhand, send it by courier to the vehicle where the encryptor and the teletype were located, have it done, and then the same courier would bring it back to me as proof that a telegram had been sent?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On a condition that the telegram was signed. There should have been a clear indication of who the author was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you perhaps know that General Tolimir, in that way, on the 13th of July, sent as many as two telegrams to the Main Staff? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that you sent any telegrams on that day. But I suppose that you had to have a certain manner of communication by telegram, or by courier, or in any other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up D55 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I have to say that this is: "The Fall of Zepa." That's the name of the document. It was drafted by Mr. Bezruchenko who was an investigator for the OTP.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please look at paragraph 59 to see that I, indeed, did send those telegrams.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let's look at paragraph 59 where it says: "During the night of 12 and 13 July 1995, VRS established contact with Colonel Palic, who was invited to arrive at the UNPROFOR check-point in the area of Boksanica." I'm sorry, I made a mistake. We need to read paragraph 60. 59 is not important. 60. And I start reading: "The meeting between VRS General Tolimir and Zepa civilian leaders Hamdija Torlak and Mujo Omanovic took place on the 13th of July at 1200 hours. According to Tolimir's account the agenda of the meeting included demililtarisation of the enclave and freedom of movement of the civilian population in accordance with Geneva Conventions as of 12 August 1949. According to the document, representatives of the local authorities in Zepa stated that they were authorised to resolve the problem of Zepa with the following guarantees: Three days for consultations with the population and the leadership in Sarajevo, movement out of all civilians and military able-bodied men, evacuation to be completed in the presence of UNPROFOR, UNHCR, and military observers guarantees of security while moving across the RS territory, a possibility to stay in Zepa for those who wish to stay." My question: Based on this expert report, is it clear that the OTP knew that Tolimir even had a meeting with Mr. Torlak on Boksanica on that day, on the 13th July, that subsequently he sent a telegram from which some of the parts were quoted in this expert report?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It derives from this that whoever had this document could see from it that on the 13th July, 1200 hours, you had a meeting with the civilian leaders of Zepa, as it says here, and that you subsequently reported to the Main Staff about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And now we can look at the telegram to see what it looks like.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is P491.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: That telegram was dispatched at 1820 hours on the same day. It was encoded, and it was sent to the Main Staff. Here is the telegram. And it bears my signature. The investigator used this telegram to extract the elements that I have just read out to you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I would like to call up 1D744. Page 42. Or, no -- rather, please, let's look at paragraph 62 in D55. I apologise to the e-court for having called up a new document. I wanted to finish with the previous document first.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now we can see paragraph 62 on the screen. Paragraph 62 in the document entitled: "The Fall of Zepa." Now you can see paragraph 62 where it says: "Later in the afternoon on the same day, on the 13th of July, Tolimir reported to General Mladic that the follow-up meeting with Torlak and Omanovic which was expected to take place at 2100 hours, did not take place. Torlak and Omanovic informed Tolimir through UNPROFOR that the government in Sarajevo had decided against moving the population out and that they were willing to secure support by majority of population for the already-taken decision to move out. They also informed the majority of the residents and soldiers that everybody would be provided with a possibility to leave or stay in Zepa if they surrender weapons and recognise Serb authority." My question is this: This telegram was sent in the late afternoon hours on 13th of July, when a new meeting, a follow-up meeting was expected to take places. Does this telegram also show that I was in communication at least twice with the Main Staff by way of telegrams?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is obvious that you sent another telegram to contact the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, could you look at paragraph 63. This paragraph was sent on the 13th of July by General Zivanovic to the Main Staff about the meeting in Zepa. He says: "We believe that the leaders of Zepa agree to move out. They are ready to move out. However their decision is under the negative influence of the leadership in Sarajevo, which has warned them through the media and through various types of communication not to accept the Serb propaganda, and that they will be adequately protected by the international community. We also believe that Muslims from Zepa use similar tactics as in Srebrenica. Probably they have made a decision to evacuate women and children in an organised way across the RS territory, and illegally send the militarily fit population into the Muslim territory. That is why they probably avoid the meeting, so as to win time to withdraw the able-bodied men." My question is this: Does this reflect the reality? Is this what really happened, as described by General Zivanovic, who also was appraised of the situation and who had also attended the meetings with the Muslim representatives? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in the area of Zepa until the 25th of July. The evacuation of women and children had already been under way. During my previous testimony to the Prosecutor's question, whether I or my unit ever entered Zepa, I answered that the units didn't enter Zepa but that I personally did and that that was the first and only time that I saw Mr. Avdo Palic. Our encounter was very brief and he told me that the military would not accept the offered variant, although they were provided a guarantees [as interpreted] but that they would rather withdraw to Zlovrh which is a trig point at 1.532 metres. And in passing, he just mentioned, Please, don't set up any ambushes for us on any of the axes. We parted ways. I was given another task. And the subsequent developments are reflected in General Zivanovic's document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you personally know Avdo Palic, since you told us what he had told you? Did he hail from the same town from which you hailed? And that you went to school together, to the secondary school?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know Mr. Palic. Having completed my elementary education, I moved to Belgrade where I attended secondary military school. I heard of him during the war. We didn't know each other. That was the one and only time when we saw each other. In view of the circumstances under which we met, I could say that that was a normal conversation. He had spoken about times before the conflict, and he said, It was all unnecessary. We will still have to live together. And then I took the opportunity and asked him, If that was not necessary, why did you attack us on the 4th of July [as interpreted]? And then I gave him all the dates from the outset of their attacks. And I told him that we responded to every fifth or sixth of their attacks when we could no longer tolerate losses. We were forced to respond. In other words, what we did were reactions to their actions. I can say here with full responsibility that if they hadn't attacked us, if they had not launched offensives against us, the VRS would have never attacked that area, because we did not have either tactical operative or strategic reasons to place that area under our control.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In your answer, you mentioned that they attacked us on the 4th of June. Could you please give us the year? And what happened, if you know? Can you do it for the transcript and for the Trial Chamber's benefit, please.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 4th of June, 1992, a unit from Pale. It was probably the 1st Romanija Brigade or at least parts thereof and that brigade had been recently established. So that unit was given a task to supply food, and water to a former JNA unit which was at the radio relay hub at Zlovrh. That was a radio relay hub of the former JNA. It was the central point of the army which served for communication with the eastern/western and all the other parts of Republika Srpska. Bearing in mind the history of the area and what both Muslims and Serbs remembered from history, an agreement had been reached between the army and the Muslim people for the army to pass freely to the radio relay hub that no fire would be open, no actions would be taken against them, and the Muslims would guarantee them free passage to go there, to fetch their belongings and to come back. That was the agreement that had been reached. The commander of the VRS unit, Major Dragan Suka, had received an order from the main -- from the Main Staff of the VRS not to fire a single bullet during that mission. The column passed through the village of Stoborane, which is a Muslim village, Godjenje, another Muslim village, Bloznje [phoen] village, another Muslim village, and when they headed towards Borak, they were ambushed, and 45 soldiers of the VRS were killed. A large number were taken prisoner. And those were the heaviest losses of the VRS, perhaps even throughout the entire war. And they happened at the very outset of the conflict and that reflected negatively on the army, and it also had a negative impact on the trust placed in the military leadership and the state leadership. The consequences of that attack may have been disastrous. That was the first conflict in the sector of Zepa in the war that took place recently in our country.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please, yesterday you saw a map, and you had a lot of objections to that map. I would like to call it up again in e-court. I would like to show you page 12, to which you had a lot of objections.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The exhibit number is P104. It was used yesterday. And I would like to focus on page 12 in e-court. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We can see the map. Please, General, tell us, while looking at the elements of the combat deployment of both side, how far is the front line from the Main Staff in kilometres? And I'm referring to the year 1995. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in 1995, I would say that it was 5 to 6 kilometres. But if you allow me, I would like to underline one thing here. The village of Krivace, where it says "Krivace IKM," is a Muslim village. Podzeplje, a Muslim village, Godjenje, a Muslim village, Podplane [phoen], where it says the base of the 65th Regiment, is also a Muslim village. That was the situation in 1992. Now where we have letters VRC and the circle and above it Han Pijesak, the village of Crna Rijeka is a Serbian village, and this particular village was evacuated in 24 hours in 52 or 53, I don't know, in order to construct a command post for the armed forces of the then country. But you see this position where Krivace is. They are virtually above this command post; whereas, I have some relatives, the Borkovic and Novakovic families in Crni Vrh, had been evacuated overnight from that area and that was the area that was actually never used much by the army. Therefore, after the fifth attack by the Muslims forces, we were forced and I was personally directing this action to move the Muslim forces from the Krivace sector because we were suffering casualties and fatalities on a daily basis. You know that Warrant Officer Zecevic was killed in July. Then two warrant officers were killed in July in Podplane. Then they killed some other civilians in another village. Then they attacked Veliki Zep. When we moved the hub from Zlovrh here, in order not for it not to be in their territory, they attacked that again. And only after a sixth attack we responded in order to protect ourselves and to move our forces from that area, just do give us some breathing space and to avoid losses that we had suffered daily.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that the Muslim, after their sixth attack on the 4th of June, 1992, until the 26th of July, 1995, were positioned 5 kilometres from the Main Staff, and the Main Staff never touched them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please go on.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I first saw 35 kilometres on the transcript, but in the meantime it was corrected into 5 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now go back, please, to the situation described in this infamous paper.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we again look at 1D744, page 42 in the Serbian, and I need lines 10 through 22. And page - thank you, Aleksander - 28 in the English. Here we see page 1 in the Serbian. There's no page 42. And that's the one I need. Thank you. We are interested in the section from lines 10 to 22. In English, it is 1 to 10. Thank you, Aleksander.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And I'm going to read it out and then ask you a question. You say: "And the second thing, the procedures that Major Malinic has to take with this group of prisoners are substantially different from what is proposed here." That was in relation to this bogus telegram that you had been shown. And then you say: "What's the difference" -- Actually the question is: "What's the difference?" And then you say: "It's different because from the moment the surrendering started, he requested from Milici a medical team to give first aid to the wounded and the hurt. He asked and he received water and food for these people. They were kept at this football field just in order to control them easier. The TV crews were allowed to film the people at the football pitch." 1 And then the Prosecutor asked you if you were there and how you knew about this, and so on and so forth. Please, you answered that you know, because you were informed of -- because you were informed of this by Mladic [as interpreted]. My question is: In the first interview conducted with you in 1995, and that goes for Malinic as well, which was conducted on 30th of July, 1995, was his answer that he never complied with it and that he had actually never seen it? I am talking about the interview of 2005, and you also said that you gave an interview in 2005. It was wrongly recorded in the transcript. Thank you, Aleksander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: There's another problem in the transcript. I suppose, on line 21 of page 15, it is recorded that you have said "because you were informed of this by Mladic." But if you read the interview on the screen, the answer of this witness was "from Major Malinic's report." I don't know if you misspoke or if it was an interpretation issue. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would also add that that information, as you've indicated came from Malinic. And at line 28 of page 28, it also indicates that the conversation in which the witness learned this occurred about a year after the event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What is your reference? You mean line 28 of page 28 of the interview, I suppose?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Of the interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. So after these interventions, Mr. Savcic, are you in the position to answer that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am. Excuse me. So, it is a well-known fact, although I don't know whether this Trial Chamber is aware of it, that in the period between the 12th of October, 1994, up to mid-June 1995, I was in hospital, following an incident in which I was seriously wounded. Practically, I did not see Malinic until the 27th of July, 1995. On that morning, of the 27th of July, I received an order from the commander of the Main Staff to urgently set off towards Drvar and to report to the chief of the Main Staff, General Milovanovic. I think that the distance is between 5- and 700 kilometres to that destination. So after such a long time, I was passing through Nova Kasaba. It was only natural for me to drop off and to see Malinic, to say hello. I spent about half an hour with him. Now if you asked me what we talked about, I would find it very difficult to answer that, but I suppose that after such a long time, we greeted each other, we inquired about each other's health. He also probably asked me how my wound was healing, et cetera, and I asked him how he faired in the previous event. So I cannot tell you certainly whether he told me this information on that occasion or on some other occasion. But I know that when we talked on that occasion, that was not mentioned. Later on when we had an opportunity and more time to discuss things, I think maybe it was mentioned. However, if we stayed together for half an hour only, I'm telling you that these were the only topics that we would have tackled in such a short time. So, in other words, nothing of substance and nothing important and relevant for the preceding event.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We've seen now what you stated in your first interview with the OTP investigators in 2005. Now let us look at what Mr. Malinic said. That is 02781, page 15 in Serbian --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is this -- Mr. Tolimir, is this a 65 ter number?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. Thank you, Mr. President. I apologise for not mentioning that. 65 ter 02781. Page 15 in Serbian, lines 14 through 28. And, in English, page 17. Thank you, Aleksander.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now let's start from line 14 which reads at the end of the sentence is -- and this is the beginning in the English.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot find the section that Mr. Tolimir is reading. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we don't receive interpretation because the interpreters need an indication where they can find the relevant part in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I said twice in English page 17, line 3. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to repeat: "This is an order that was not signed and if it is original, as you say, it has to be signed. Whatever arrives by tape is not signed. Secondly, it says that the prisoners be put away, away from the express way or something, and be placed in detention facility. As a senior officer, I had to carry out the order that I received from my superior, and I had to do everything in order to carry out the order. Since members of the 28th Division ... were the whole time, until the transport, that is, until they entered the buses and the truck in the soccer field, they did not change position anywhere. And that happened in late afternoon. Had I received this order, and I see that it was received at 1510, I had to act according to it and carry out this order. Since all the detainees were at the stadium and were not relocated anywhere until they entered the buses and trucks, either -- that means that either I did not receive the telegram or that I did not carry out the order. As a soldier, I had to carry out the order."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: On the basis of this, I would like to ask you the following: Since you know what this is all about, can you tell us, does this reflect the fact that Mr. Malinic, during his first interview with the OTP, clearly told the Prosecutors what was happening in Kasaba where the captured Muslims from the 28th Division on retreat were handed over or taken away in Nova Kasaba?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can see here that Major Malinic is suspicious about the authenticity of this document, and he doubts the fact whether he had received that document or not. He is rather inclined to the option that he had not, in fact, received that document. Was there any other question within your question? Because, perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: No, thank you. That would be enough. On page 47 of the transcript, line 5, of the conversation when Malinic, in this case, he said that he would not basically make any amendments to what he said in 2005, and that was in response to the Prosecutor question whether he would give basically the same answers, and he said, I wouldn't change anything in respect to what I said in 2005. My question is: Are you aware that when he testified in his case, he virtually confirmed everything that he said back in 2005?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sorry I interrupted you. please wait. Mr. Tolimir, can you please repeat the page number of the transcript - this is not recorded - so that can be found. And after that, you should start with your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The date is 8th of June, 2011. According to my notes, it's page 47, line 5. I don't know whether, in the meantime, the number of the page has been changed. This is what I quoted right now, and this is what he said on page 47, and that is, I wouldn't basically change anything that I said back in 2005. So my question is, let's me repeat it for the benefit of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is not necessary. If the witness recalls the question, then it's fine. He should answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I remember, the question was whether I knew what Malinic stated in this trial, here; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes. The question is: Are you aware, whether Malinic, when testifying in this trial, as I indicated on the 8th of June, did he state that he stood by the statement he made in 2005, speaking to the investigators?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, because I did not follow the trial. So I don't know what he stated on what issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. That's the reason why I quoted to you from what he said so you could see. Thank you for that answer. We won't be discussing this any further. Do you know that the Prosecution had this document also reviewed by an expert in graphology?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To make it clear to everyone, can we see P125.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is: Do you know that the OTP had this document tested by a graphological expert, and the expert said that this document had not been drafted on the machine used by the Rogatica Brigade?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. First, I don't believe that was the conclusion of the expert at all. And if General Tolimir has a specific cite that can he refer to that would be helpful in identifying it. But I don't believe that that's the case. I think that either there's a translation error or General Tolimir is mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, are you able to give a reference to the expert report, or the testimony of the expert?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. That's the expert report of Witness Kathryn Barr. P1972, 61 through 63. Thank you Aleksander.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My reply to the question involving the expert report on this document would be that I don't know anything about it. I'm not aware of any expertise or report.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see P1972, pages 61 through 63.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Are you referring to pages or to paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I meant paragraphs 61 through 63.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: They are now on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This summary. Quoting from paragraph 6.1: "The similarities between typing on documents 0425-8580 and 0441-0981, are such that, in my opinion, there is conclusive evidence that they were both produced by the same machine. "Although there is a difference in the position of the red colouration associated with the typing on document 0441-0992 compared to that on documents 0425-8580 and 0441-0981, there are also significant similar layers such as in the defect in the lower case p that I could not consider could have occurred by chance. In my opinion, these similarities provide strong evidence that document 0441-0992 was produced by the same machine that produced documents 0425-8580 and 0441-0981. "The difference in the position of the red colouration could have been caused by the ribbon being moved between the typing of 0441-0981 and that of document 0441-0992." Paragraph 6.3: "The differences between the typing of document 0441-0972 and that of the other three documents are such that, in my opinion, there is conclusive evidence that document 0441-0972 was typed on a different machine to the other three documents." Let us look at P125. Those are the same documents, same numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, referring to your last question, I don't see any indication that we can draw a conclusion from the expert report to your -- as you did in your question, that this document has not been drafted on the machine used by the Rogatica Brigade. There's no mention of any brigade in this expert report. If you want to put a question in relation to that to the witness, you should rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Savcic, tell us, did you and your unit have a typewriter while you were in combat operations in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Neither there, nor on any other location, was a typewriter one of the things I worked with.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Does that mean that these documents had to be typewritten on the machines of the Rogatica Brigade and the machines used by their encryption officers?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was in that area at this time, we used exclusively their resources, their machines. There was no one else, no other unit of the Army of Republika Srpska. Only the Rogatica Brigade was there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see P520, page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you tell us if this document was done by a teletype or a typewriter? It's page 2 in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document was processed by a teletype. Ah, the one we see now, this second page, is not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have P520 back.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see P520 again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, it is on the screen. But we have page 2 of the screen -- on the screen. But do you want to see page 1? Then you should ask for it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, page 1. The teletype document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let's look at a document. It's better for you to say this. I'll just ask. What is the difference between this document and the document we saw a second ago, the one written on a typewriter?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The difference is that it was produced by a different machine. This document on the right was produced on an ordinary typewriter, I suppose the kind that was used before, before computers appeared. Whereas, the left one was processed by a teletype. And the differences between the two are significant. This one is properly recorded with the number of the protocol in a different place. The protocol number on the other one is at the top, and to be quite honest, I never watched signalsmen at work, so I don't know how they do their work. But you can see there are significant differences. You can easily distinguish with minimum military training between a document done -- produced by a teletype and a document produced by the typewriter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: For the sake of the record, to have a full understanding of the last answer, we have on the screen on the left side, page 1 of P520, the B/C/S version; and on the right side of the screen, page 2 of this document this -- in B/C/S. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since you now see both pages, can you tell me which is a teletype document and which is not?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document on the left was produced by teletype. The number at the top is 0441-0971. That's the teletype document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see, instead of that, P125. Or perhaps we can place it instead of the right one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The document on the left, is it a teletype document?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, to the right of this document, we already got it, what I wanted to ask for. How do you distinguish between these two documents? How do you see the difference?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an evident difference in format. You don't have to be an expert in this area to observe the obvious differences. It's obvious that those two documents were produced on two different machines. It's quite evident that two different machines, devices, call them what you like, were used to produce these two documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you see that even the graphologist said that these two documents were produced on two different machines? If you were listening when I was quoting from the graphologist report.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He mentioned some documents - I can't remember the numbers now - but I remember the report said two different machines were used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The reason I'm on my feet is that the expert report of Dr. Barr doesn't refer to the document 0441-0971, which is on the right hand of the screen in e-court at the moment, as compared to 0425-8580 which is on the left-hand side of the screen at the moment. But she does refer to the document 0441-0972, which was previously on the screen in e-court, as compared to the document which is P125 on the left-hand side of the screen. And she distinguishes between those two documents. So perhaps if General Tolimir wants to show the witness P -- I'm sorry, 0441-0972 that would be a more appropriate comparison for the witness to make, in terms of the expert report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we have that document on the right side of the screen, please. Now we have these documents on the screen. Mr. Tolimir, continue, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hello. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: These documents, in terms of paper and the contents, were they teletyped?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now instead of this document on the right, could we display P520, page 1. These documents are not different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We all want to have a good and clear record. If you say "these documents are not different," you should make it clear to which documents you are referring so that the witness is able to follow, and the Chamber is able to follow.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Savcic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused repeat the number of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The document on the left-hand side, does it differ from the document that we see on the right-hand side, and what differences do you discern between the two documents?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just told you a minute ago that the two documents differ. At first glance, you can see that they were produced on different machines. The left side document was typed on a regular typewriter. The right-hand side document 0441-1971 was teletyped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: For the record, on the left-hand side of the screen, we have 0425-8580. That was not recorded.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I wanted to display two documents which differ in terms of their formats as well as their contents. They were both analysed by experts and they were produced on two different machines. The left-hand side document 0425-8580, what is this? Is this a type written document or is it an electronic print of the document?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was produced on a regular typewriter. There is no trace of a teletyping machine on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you please look at 0441-0971 what is this? Was this produced on a regular typewriter or on a teletyping machine? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second document shows the traces of a teletype machine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, would anybody who is looking and comparing be able to discern a clear difference between a document produced by a regular typewriter, as opposed to a document produced by a teletyping machine? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everybody who has had at least one opportunity to see a document produced by a regular typewriter as opposed to a teletype document can see a difference and can easily conclude how the document was produced.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. General, sir, did you and Mr. Malinic point out that particular difference during your first respective interviews with the OTP in 2005? I have already quoted that, and I have already displayed that.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We pointed out that fact, amongst others.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to call 02781, page 13 in Serbian, lines 32 through 33, and page 15 in English. And my legal assistants will give you the exact line numbers once the page is displayed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I take it that this is a 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct. I apologise, once again. Thank you, Mr. President. It a 65 ter document. Page 13 in Serbian, please. Thank you. Lines 32 and 33. Thank you. Aleksander, could you please give us the exact line numbers in English. It is page 15 in English.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Just for the record, this is 65 ter document 2781. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And this is the OTP statement of the Witness Malinic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Again, we are looking at line 30 where Mr. Malinic says, so without a quote, and he is talking about the document that we previously saw. And then the Prosecutor asks him: "And can you remember what -- where the TV crews were ordered from?" Answer was: "I think that it was from the command of the regiment and to allow these TV crews to tape or to record whatever they wished to. So, you now, without any censorship."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we move to the following page in Serbian, page 14. And the English can stay. Thank you, Aleksander.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And now the question: "And did that TV crews, in fact, arrive? "A. Yes and they shot, they recorded. And then the Prosecutor asks: "And can you remember what TV crews they were, from what news channels, from what journalistic companies?" And then Malinic says: "I think that there were some foreign TV crews and also a crew from Radio-Television Srpska. So at least three teams all together. And since we received the order that we were to allow them to tape anything, there was no need to control them, to check their IDs or anything. They all arrived together, all the three teams. As far as I can remember, I believe that they did their job. As far as I can remember, they even interviewed people who were detained at the stadium, who were captured. I really can't remember exactly which TV crews they were." My question to you is this: This is how things transpired, according to Mr. Malinic. He had received an order from the command of the regiment. My question is this: Did Mr. Malinic always obey orders? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of a single instance where he did differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. My question: If those TV crews, both local and foreign, filmed the detainees and interviewed them, my question is this: Was it then possible that the general public was informed about the events in Nova Kasaba?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that that was the reason why they had been taped in the first place, to be presented to the general public. I don't see any other reason why they should have been taped.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If the Main Staff, on the 13th, through the command of the regiment, order Malinic to receive TV crews and to allow them to film, does that mean that on the 13th, the Main Staff wanted to document the events and inform the general public truthfully about what had transpired? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be the only logical conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, it is time for our first break. We must have our first break now and will resume quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Could I call up 65 ter 02099 in e-court. We would like to see it to be able to use it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: While we are waiting, I would like to say that this document was issued by the Main Staff of the VRS on 13th of July, 1995. And it was sent to all commands, including the command of the 65th Protection Motorised Regiment. It was sent to all the units of the Drina Corps, as you can see, and the document is entitled: "Preventing leakage of military secrets in the area of combat operations order." And I quote from the introductory part into the order: "In order to ensure the organised conduct of planned combat operations and other activities in the general sectors of Srebrenica and Zepa, and in order to prevent the leakage of confidential information classified as military secrets, I hereby order ..." Under 1: "By means of planned and organised control, prevent the entry of all uninvited individuals to the area of combat operations in the general sector of Srebrenica and Zepa." My question is this: Is this in keeping with the rules of combat? I mean, bullet point 1. And what can you tell us about this?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first bullet point of this order is absolutely in keeping with the rules of combat, which specify that military commander or a unit commander is duty-bound to evacuate or prevent entry to all uninvited individuals from an area of combat activities, if they are not involved in combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And what about bullet points 2 and 3? Do they specify how unknown individuals should be prevented from entering the area of combat? For example, by setting up check-points. You, yourself, were involved in such activities before the war and during the war, so would you be able to tell us whether what you see in bullet point 2 and 3 is customary?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is absolutely commonplace, and it is based on the situation at hand, as well as on the rules and regulations that regulate such situations; i.e., it is based on the conclusions arising from the assessments of the current situation, as well as on the rules and regulations that regulate that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's look at bullet point 4 where it says: "In the area of combat operations in the general areas of Srebrenica and Zepa, prevent the entry of all local and foreign journalists, except for the journalists of the press centre of Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska." My question is this: Did the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, due to combat activities, have the right to prevent the entry of journalists, except for those who were affiliated with the press centre of the Main Staff? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you -- you can see that in the -- in the introduction to this order, in order to prevent the leakage of intelligence and other confidential information, only journalists affiliated with the press centre of the Main Staff of the VRS are allowed to enter it, because they are the only ones that are fully under control, and they do not inform the general public, but, rather, they gather information for the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was this order sent by telegram; and can you see that when you look at the document? Can you conclude by just looking at the document how it was sent?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was sent by telegram.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, did the Protection Regiment, your own unit, also receive this document? We see that your regiment is one of the addressees.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here that a telegram was also sent to the Protection Regiment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could e-court now display 2085.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And what about this document? Are you tendering it, Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I tender this document. Thank you for reminding me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 2099 shall be assigned Exhibit D286. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now see in e-court 2085. If we could just turn it around.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now we see this order. There is a stamp at the top instead of the heading. It says, "Command of the Motorised Protection Regiment." Now can you see it?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It says, "Command of the Motorised Protection Regiment." The date is 15 July 1995. And it's properly recorded. It says: "Order for prevention of leakage of secret military information in the zone of combat operations." It says: "In order to carry out the planned combat operations in an organised way and prevent outflow, that is to say, leakage of confidential military information," which are a military secret, "I hereby order, certain measures ..." And it says, "Commander Lieutenant-Colonel Milomir Savcic." In fact, on his behalf, it was signed by Jazic, who was on the command post.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we scroll down to see the signature and stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was this document sent exclusively to units of the Protection Regiment?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We see the English translation on the right-hand side, it does not contain the word "for" next to the signature. It makes it look like you signed it. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the English language, but, yes, it says "signature" at the bottom. We clearly see that the document was signed by my Deputy Chief of Staff, because I was not at the command post. I was in the field, in combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is it clearly written in the same letters and the same pen as the signature. Does it say "for" and then below "Jovo Jazic"? Do you know that signature?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Jazic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put a question to the witness. Is it perhaps possible that you mark with a pen, with the assistance of the usher -- it should be enlarged again, the signature block. Thank you. And the usher could please assist the witness. Could you please indicate where we can see the handwritten word "for"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. And could you please tell me, what -- the handwritten name, could you please read that into the record?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Handwritten, last and first names, in that sequence, is Jazic, Jovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What was the position of this Mr. Jazic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Jazic was deputy commander of the Protection Regiment, and, at the same time, Chief of Staff. He was authorised to sign documents in the absence of the commander. We saw a document yesterday from the time when I was undergoing treatment, and on that document, it was not formulated as "for the commander"; but, "standing in for the commander." However, in this case, I was in command of the regiment. I was just not there at the command post, and he was signing for me. That's in accordance with the rules and that's the common practice in all units of the army from the level of squad to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that clarification. Mr. Tolimir, I would like to invite you to tender this marked document so that we have it clear where we can find this -- this marked word. Are you tendering it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to tender this document, on which the witness marked the words "za," meaning "for" before the signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This document, with the marking, will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 2085, marked by the witness in court, shall be assigned Exhibit D287. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Tolimir, are you tendering the plain document in addition to that marked one?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would also like to tender it without the marking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter document 2085 -- shall be assigned Exhibit D288. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please carry on, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: General, please tell us, this order of the Protection Regiment which we see on the left-hand side in Serbian, was it written based on the order of the Main Staff concerning the same activities that the Prosecutor introduced under 65 ter number 02099?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Looking at the contents of the document, we see it was written based on an order of the Main Staff. However, below this heading, which says, "Prevent leakage of confidential information," my deputy was supposed to write the following: "Pursuant to the order," such and such "of the Main Staff." That's how he should have written it, but he omitted that. However, from the list of activities ordered to be taken, it is clear that this follows from the order of the crisis -- of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was it really necessary to write several orders on the same activities; for instance, to Major Mandic [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The transcript reads Major Mandic. It should be Malinic. And the answer to your question is a that there was absolutely no need to write more than one order concerning one and the same activities. There was no need for repetition. If there were new tasks signed, it would have been different. Then it would have been possible to write several orders in the course of one day, if the situation required it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Look now at this order before you, just to see if all the three-points are the same ones as contained as in 65 ter 02099, which has become D286.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Aleksander. Thank you. Mr. President, since we looked at both orders and admitted them into evidence, would you allow the right-hand page to be replaced by the document we've just admitted and marked so that the witness can see the difference?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: On the right-hand side, D288, please, in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: General, looking at item 1 of this order, and item 2, and item 1 of the second order, are they almost identical? Do they deal with the same thing?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please look at item 2 now. Is it present in the order on the right-hand side? Was the item 2 from the Main Staff order conveyed in the regiment's order?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: What about point 3?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Item 4. Is it identical to item 2 in the regiment's order?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Item 5 of the Main Staff order, is it identical to item 3 of the order of the command of the 65th Motorised Protection Regiment?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can we see from this that this order by the regiment's command was written based on the order of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we can see that. We can see that the document on the right-hand side follows from the document on the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We have no further questions on these documents. We will now move to the next set of questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now display in e-court P1434, page 4. Let's look at page 1 first, and this is page 4. We can just look at page 1 for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We see this is a document in the form of telegram from the 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade that was also referred to as the Rogatica Brigade, security and intelligence organ. And the heading reads: "Information about prisoners of war in the holding centre at Rogatica." Let's look at all the points in this document, 1, 2, 3, and 4. Or, rather, let's look at the list. We see 25 names of prisoners on page 1.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move to the next page. I kindly ask e-court to display the next page. Thank you. We see there there is a total of 45 of prisoners of war registered at the holding centre in Rogatica. Can we move to the next page. Thank you. Next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Under point (b) we see the health status of the prisoner of wars. And point 3, treatment. It says, point (c): "Treatment. In keeping with the order of General Tolimir and his instructions, the necessary measures have been taken to the extent of our abilities, and these are mainly observed," among other things. It says: "The sick prisoners have been separated from the healthy ones and they were placed in three different rooms ..." Let look at the next page, listing problems. The page in English is the same. Here we see: "Problems. During the evacuation of the civilian population from Zepa carried out in the morning of 28th July and the separation of military conscripts from the group of Muslims, in the area of the elementary school on the Tiska-Kladanj road, during the inspection and search, money was taken from the following Muslims ..." And then we see a list of names an amounts: "Total seized, (stolen) 25 US dollars and 1800 Deutschemark. The said Muslims complained to General Tolimir (and me) saying this was done by people commanded by a short swarthy man wearing a black beret and who was limping." And then it says: "It is obvious that this was Lieutenant Matic, who at the moment of separation of the Muslims came to the spot -- came to the scene and carried out searches in the school and in the school compound. "General Tolimir demands that this case be investigated and the money found." Since you looked yesterday at the document that you know well, do you now understand why investigation was started against Lieutenant Matic; and can you tell the Trial Chamber about it?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's clear from this that it was your order that instructed them to inquire into the matter and take measures against the offender. I believe he was later expelled from the military police, and I don't know if he was punished in any other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see Prosecution 65 ter 07367.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: That was shown to you during the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Just for the record, this is Exhibit P2427. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to thank the Registrar. I apologise for not having prepared this number earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now you can see the document issued by the Main Staff. Yesterday you were asked whether there are any influences on the investigation, or is there an interference with the investigation? Is there any interference on the investigation by the organs of your Protection Regiment; or is it the case that they are forwarded information from other organs which were not within the authority of the security organ and the military police of the 65th Motorised Protection Regiment? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see any form of interference with the investigation. When you used the term "interfering with an investigation," I understand this as some sort of an instruction or an order which channels or directs an investigation, which is positive and allowed, or, rather, prevents an investigation, which is not allowed, and which should be punished. This is just a piece of information about a member of the police battalion at the time. To be honest, I didn't know about this. If I'd been there when this Matic arrived in the Protection Regiment, but if I had been there, he would not have joined us, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In paragraph 2, do you see that Lieutenant Beara says that it is obvious that Matic lied when he said that he did not confiscate money from the detainees, and there are testimonies by soldiers to prove it. Does this mean that whoever sent this document also confirms in it that Matic, indeed, lied?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may be concluded from this document that Matic had previously given a statement about those circumstances and that in that statement of yours, he had denied everything. However, through further operative work, further proof was obtained that he was, indeed, involved in the things that he denied, and there were documents to that effect. In other words, eye-witnesses' testimonies proved that -- that Lieutenant Matic lied, and what followed was a normal procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to the following page in the same document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Does this document specify that evidence is attached to this document in the form of bank notes that Lieutenant Matic took away from the detainees, as well as the statements provided by the soldiers? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This proves that he both committed the crime and the enclosed documents also show how he committed it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now can we go to the following page. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We see it now. The command of the Drina Corps sent this document on the 6th of August, eight days after I had given my verbal order, and it says: "Attached, we are sending you the statement of military policemen who were present during the robbing of the Balija." Is this another proof of the misdeed committed by Lieutenant Matic?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is proof of his crime and measures taken.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the e-court produce the following page of the same document, please, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We see a document issued by the 1st Vlasenica Brigade. This is a statement by a soldier who witnessed the incident when Matic took money. You saw that yesterday. Does this also prove that evidence was also submitted by the Vlasenica Brigade that was on the strength of the Drina Corps? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is another proof of that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show the following statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Another one that you saw yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 7 in English. Thank you, Aleksandar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Again, the command of the 1st Vlasenica Brigade Command. Provides a statement by Desimir Vasiljevic. Yesterday, you were shown this document by the Prosecutor. Does it -- this also constitute a piece of evidence of the crime committed by Matic? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. My question is this: Were measures taken when crimes against prisoners of war were detected?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions about this particular topic. Thank you. We're now going to look at document - thank you, Aleksander - P2433. Thank you. We can see the document that you were shown yesterday by the Prosecutor. Since you have already read this document, can you tell us whether here General Tolimir sent you a document here to inform you that he had been invited by the president because of the contents that he quoted from bullet point 1 through bullet point 4, as was quoted to the president of the republic in the document submitted to him by the Dutch embassy. Is it clear that the entire content of the document from 1 through 4 is under quotation marks? Everything starting with "on 13th July, 1995, persons from a list of 239 refugees," and so on and so forth. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told the Prosecutor yesterday that I had never seen the document before, although it is addressed to myself. However, I don't remember ever having seen this document. However, it is not in dispute that you drafted this document, based on another document sent to you by the Dutch embassy that you discussed that previous document with the president of the republic, and that based on that, you sent information or a report to me as the then-chief of administration, and that is all that I can tell you about this document as I sit here today.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, for the record, whether it was a duty of every single officer to inform his command or the Main Staff if he had been invited to come to the president of the republic's office and discuss a certain thing with him? Was he duty-bound to inform his superiors of the contents of such a conversation or such an invitation? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a rule, a military officer has to inform his superior command about every contact with a higher or a more superior level of command at the request of such a superior level of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did they do that in keeping with the rules, and did I inform the Main Staff about my contact? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You did everything by the book. The rules that were in force at the time had been adopted from the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please look at the penultimate paragraph after what we see here as the last sentence where it says: "I informed madam president that I knew that all civilians had been evacuated from Potocari in co-operation with UNPROFOR and the ICRC but that their names were never recorded because over 10.000 to 15.000 persons were evacuated in accordance with the agreement that was signed by the leadership of Zepa and UNPROFOR Commander Rupert Smith with the representatives of the Army of Republika Srpska." My question is this: To all those who watched television and read newspapers, was it well-known what I wrote in this letter and what agreement was signed with Mr. Rupert Smith?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is a well-known fact that the media, including electronic and printed media, covered this event extensively, so that event was well-known.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In the following paragraph, do you see my assessment? And then in the next paragraph, do you see my proposals?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And, finally, do I suggest at the end of the text that the chief of the General Staff should be informed about the contents of this document; i.e., was this document meant to be public, and was it meant to be conveyed to the chief of the General Staff? I quote from the document where I say in the last sentence in the English version - thank you, Aleksander -: "I suggest that the chief of the General Staff be informed of this document?"

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Your suggestions are clearly visible, and they include your last suggestion, that the chief of the General Staff should be informed about things that were happening, and you probably wanted to apply that to some future similar situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In war, did individuals repeat some things, did they repeat some requests and wishes? And when they did that, they often mentioned that they had informed the superior command of those requests and wishes. They then wrote about that in their memoirs in order to create conditions for a public recognition of such documents, which were subsequently created based on the memory of those who allegedly created them. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is clearly a very broad question. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That is my objection, Mr. President. It is a bit vague, and I ask for General Tolimir, perhaps, to rephrase it in a manner that is a bit more comprehensive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your question can mean everything and nothing, especially, "We will repeat some things, did they repeat some requests and wishes." That can relate to everything. If you want to receive a correct and precise answer, you should put a specific question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]
