utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In order to receive a concrete question without me leading the witness, I'm going to read paragraph 2 that we see on the screen in the Serbian, and we also see it in English. "I suggest that the legalisation of this list not be allowed, both for legal reasons and because it was compiled from Mr. Nuhanovic's memory and because anyone could have been included on the list, even people who had been evacuated in an organised manner or had gone missing prior to the evacuation during combat operations." My question is this, and it is based on what I have just read out: Did I, indeed, suggest that the legalisation of this and similar lists should be disallowed for legal reasons and for the fact that they were compiled from memory? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this is precisely the issue here. I have been following you, your questions, I have been reading the documents, so I assume that this was the beginning of a future database that would contain the names of the killed and missing persons. All the three parties to the conflict did that after the war, so this was just an attempt for us to pay attention to the fact that documents which were created subsequently after the war, from memory, documents without any valid foundations, documents which were not created when events were unfolding. What I'm saying is that after a certain while, after a lapse of time, it is very difficult to remember things. For example, I had a command -- the commander of a squad who could never remember the names of all his ten soldiers. He could barely get to number two, and for the life of him, he couldn't remember the rest of them. I believe that will we should follow the same logic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please look at the last paragraph before my suggestion where it says: "All persons potentially interested in this topic should be spoken to personally and instructed to look for refugees or missing persons through commissions for the exchange and search for refugees or missing persons." My question is this: Did I try to cover up anything in this document? Did I hide anything from the president, from the administration, or whoever; or did I actually properly inform them about the events and proposed my suggestions to them? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think the question, as it's phrased, is practically rhetorical. And I don't think it is within the ken of this witness to answer this question, particularly in light of the fact that he claims to have absolutely no knowledge of it and no recollection of having received it. I don't see how he is in a position to answer the question, whether or not this accused hid anything in this document, because if he did, it certainly wouldn't be in the document. So I don't really see any point to that question, and I object to it on that basis. It is not relevant or probative of any salient issue before the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm convinced that this witness is able and capable to answer such a question, although he stated yesterday and today that he doesn't know this document at all and the not the circumstances in which it was created. Sir, are you able to answer the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's hard to answer the question whether something was covered up. I really cannot speculate. But, by the same token, I have no reason to suspect that anything was held back in this document. I have no way of claiming one way or another, but I can see from this last paragraph, as I concluded yesterday, it concerns an attempt to create a database on missing persons. So it's hard to say. How could I know? General Tolimir had a very important position involving many responsibilities, and he was receiving a lot of information. It's hard to say why he wrote something at a certain moment, but I suppose he wrote this because he thought he should inform the security administration. It's not hard. It's impossible to say whether somebody shared everything they knew. There are many questions that arise about what, about whom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: One moment. First, thank you for this answer. Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I just need to take you back to the last question. And I put it this way: On the basis of the excerpts that have been quoted to you from this document, are you able to make an opinion or a conclusion that the accused person might have hidden anything from the president, from the administration, or whoever he addressed, on the basis of the excerpts that have been quoted to you from this document? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm absolutely unable to conclude that he was holding back, or hiding, or covering anything up. You would have to know the entire subject matter in every detail to draw such a conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: General, did you have the ability to check in your administration with the president of the republic what I had discussed with him, what I had told him, and was he also able to check what I had told you as chief of that administration? In other words, what I had written in my report to your security organs, because you didn't see this.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no doubt that it could all have been checked. But it's also true that, now, and even less then, I would hardly be inclined to double-check on what you did, wrote, reported, et cetera. You enjoyed the reputation of a great professional, and I would not have had such doubts. But if doubts existed, of course, the possibility to check what you discussed with the president of the republic existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I'm sorry but in a private session there was even one witness who was at Potocari, testified that he did not give the lists to the Army of Republika Srpska, fearing that something might happen to the soldiers. But we won't waste any more time. That's just another proof that the lists were not given to the Army of Republika Srpska. Please, in the course of examination-in-chief, the Prosecutor asked you more than once about resubordination. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us please look at a document in e-court. It's D129. It comes from the Ministry of the Interior. The office of the minister sent it to the listed addressees on the 10th of July, 1995. It says: "Pursuant to the order of the supreme commander of the armed forces in Republika Srpska and in order to crush the enemy offensive that is under way from the safe area of Srebrenica, I hereby order, detach a part of the MUP forces," et cetera, et cetera. And then we see Ljubisa Borovcanin. I designate Ljubisa Borovcanin, deputy commander of the special police brigade as commander of the MUP units. That's the gist of the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is this: Can we see from this order to whom and why the Ministry of Interior resubordinated the special brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It must have been a slip of the tongue when you said defence minister. It's the minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first point says "detach the forces." Point 2 lists which forces. And point 3 designates the commander of these forces. From these three points, we can't see anything about resubordination. Let me look at the rest. Item 5 says the commander of the unit is required to make contact on arrival at destination with the Drina Corps Chief of Staff, General Krstic. Mr. Sladojevic, I think, is asking that we can consult about this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Savcic. Mr. Savcic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just finish this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Savcic, this is not up to Mr. Sladojevic to ask you to consult. But if you want to consult him, you may indicate that. It must be your request. But if Mr. Tolimir is not going further with this document, perhaps there is no need for that. What is your position, Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will continue because I implied that this resubordination from -- from the -- the line that says he is supposed to report to General Krstic as soon as he arrives. But I don't mind if he wants to consult with Mr. Sladojevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Savcic, do you want to consult Mr. Sladojevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Have you any idea about the time you need for the consultation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly. A couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We will adjourn for a couple of minutes, and we will wait for your indication, and then we will come back to the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to ask the parties if perhaps it is better to have our second break now and then you may use the time to consult Mr. Sladojevic, and then we will continue. Do you agree, Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I agree. We will continue talking about the resubordination of MUP units to the army, so it would really be good if Mr. Savcic could take the opportunity to consult with Mr. Sladojevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That's fine. We must have our second break then now, and we will resume at ten minutes before 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Savcic, I take it you had the opportunity to consult Mr. Sladojevic, and now you are well-prepared for the remainder of the cross-examination. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Before we begin, I'd forgotten to tender 65 ter 02781. That's the statement of Mr. Malinic, and we used some pages from it today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I would like to ask you if it's perhaps more practical only to tender those pages you have used during the examination of Mr. Savcic. The whole document contains more than 40 pages. It's a lot. And you didn't deal with them. And it was not tendered through the witness himself when he testified. Would that be a way to deal with it? Because I think you -- most of the statement of Mr. Malinic was read into the record today by you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. That part was not admitted because he had to leave early, before the weekend. But I agree with you. We can admit only those pages from the transcript that refer to my -- that are related to my questions. I don't mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: After consideration of your first motion to admit the whole document, the Chamber decided to admit the whole OTP statement of Witness Malinic into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 2781 shall be assigned Exhibit D289. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Savcic, do I need to repeat my question, or you can answer it? The question was: Can this be considered resubordination if forces are placed in the zone of the corps?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We had a situation where in other zones, such as Treskavica, where you were, MUP forces were resubordinated to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. There were MUP forces there, and the forces of the 65th Motorised Protection Regiment. And they were both resubordinated to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. And I know for sure, although I can't remember the exact name, there was one mixed, that is, combined brigade, from the 1st Krajina Corps. All these forces were resubordinated to the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. My question, following up on your answer, is: Were all soldiers individually to the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, or were they still subordinated to their own commanders, commanders of their own units, and the units, as such, were resubordinated to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A unit is resubordinated, in this case to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, and that means that the commander of that unit receives combat assignments from the commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps; whereas, soldiers and commanding officers are subordinated to their own unit commander. It's not just one section, the discipline squad, or a platoon or a company that is resubordinated to the corps command. It's just that the unit commander receives a specific combat assignment from the corps command as to what their unit is supposed to -- in the area of responsibility of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber whether disciplinary and other sanctions are something that their unit commander is authorised to take and decide on, in keeping with his powers as commander?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Any and all powers that a unit commander has before resubordination he keeps after resubordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Even if units from the Republic of Serbian Krajina were relocated in Trnovo - I don't know if you heard about that - they were called the Skorpions?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This applies to all units. At that time I was not aware of that unit in the Sarajevo theatre of war, but later on, perhaps I learned from the work of the Tribunal and from media reports that, for a while, they were in the area of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was that unit in the area, in the zone of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, as part of the MUP of the Republic of Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know that, from that time. But from what I learned later, it seems to me they were there as part of the MUP of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, the RSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You have probably heard that those Skorpions from the MUP of the Serbian Krajina committed certain crimes in Trnovo away from the combat lines on an assignment given them by their commander. Have you heard about that?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned that from media reports, again, I believe at the time when the former president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and President of Serbia, Slobodan Milosevic, was tried before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was the entire public, including all those who were in the territory in the same area as the 65th Regiment, made aware of it long after this unit left the area of Trnovo?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already said in my previous answer when I learned about it. But I suppose that most other soldiers and commanding officers who were, at that time, in the area of Trnovo, and I said also in one of my previous questions [as interpreted] that I was not aware of that unit in the Sarajevo theatre of war in the area of Trnovo. It's obvious that they were involved in some quite different things, and what they did is something that real soldiers do not do. That is, some sort of pathology.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since you heard, along with the rest of the public, what they had done, my question is: Was their arrests the responsibility of somebody in the Army of Republika Srpska when it was found they were guilty of a crime, or was it the responsibility of the command, or the state authorities of the territory which is -- who are responsible for them? Can you tell us, from your professional point of view?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's known that the first person who should have become aware of the crime they had committed is their commander, and it would be logical to expect him to take the first steps to punish that act. So it's my opinion that it's primarily, or first and foremost, the responsibility of the unit commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since the commander himself has been tried, because he gave the orders for that crime, is it then possible that the responsibility lies with the authorities of the territory to whom that unit belonged and who covered up the crime?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'm not sure what the gist of the question is but it sounds to me like General Tolimir is looking for a legal conclusion to be drawn from this witness, which I don't think is of any relevance whatsoever to the Trial Chamber. Furthermore, the determination of another Tribunal as to the facts and circumstances or findings that that Tribunal has made concerning those events in Trnovo is also of limited, if any, probative value to the Trial Chamber. So General Tolimir's question in this context, I think, has no probative value whatsoever and is largely irrelevant to the issues before the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to ask you, sir, the following question that could resolve the problem: Do you know anything about the structure of the Skorpions, their subordination to any other superior unit of the police or the army, of any army? Do you know anything about the command structure above the Skorpions in 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I know absolutely nothing about the structure of the Skorpions, the so-called Skorpions. I have no idea what they were, and the first time I heard about them was during the trial of President Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think this clarifies the situation, Mr. Tolimir, especially which kind of questions you could put to the witness with a certain expectation to get more information from him in relation to the Skorpions. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to respond to the objection of the Prosecutor. I wasn't asking about legal responsibility. I asked the General, as an experienced commander in both police forces and security forces, can police authorities have any responsibility for perpetrators when it's only five years later that they find out about the perpetrators, when the perpetrators are already in the territory of another state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm not persuaded that this witness is the best expert to -- to give you an answer about possibilities of police units to investigate certain crimes. But we are interested in your view and your opinion, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My opinion with regard to the specific issue is this: Nobody could take any measures against perpetrators of a crime if they learned about that particular crime only five years later; whereas, the perpetrators of the crime were in the territory of another state. And law enforcement agencies of one state could not be responsible for what is going on in another state. If I understood General Tolimir properly, that would be my opinion about the whole matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General, sir. This is exactly what I wanted. I wanted to hear your opinion; nothing else. Now I will let you know what happened to the -- these men.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to call up P1437. This is a judgement issued on the 10th April 2007 from the district court in Belgrade, War Crimes Chamber, in the Republic of Serbia, in Belgrade. The perpetrators are Skorpions and the crime happened while they were in Trnovo. Can we see 93 in Serbian and 125 in English, please. Thank you. I'm going to read the second paragraph that is displayed. I'm not going to read the first two lines of the paragraph that spills over from the previous page. It is the last page [as interpreted] in English on the page that is displayed. Thank you, Aleksander. And I'm reading: "From the statement of Witness Milan Milovanovic, former assistant internal affairs minister of the so-called Republic of Serbian Krajina which the Court accepted as logical and conclusive, given by a person who was, by virtue of the duty he was performing at the time, in a position to provide the Court with the most information in relation to the Skorpions unit in terms of when, on whose order the unit was formed and also when and how it was disbanded. It was established that the Skorpions unit had the status of a special unit of the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina as of 1993, and that it was deployed to the Trnovo front line in late June 1995 by the Republic of Serbian Krajina government as assistance at the prior invitation of the Republika Srpska Supreme Command."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is this: Now that you have heard what I have just read out, do you understand whose unit this was? Can you tell us, for the record, how you understood the paragraph that I have just read out from the judgement?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After having listened to your reading, I understood that that unit was a unit of the Army of Republic of Serbian Krajina that was set up in 1993 with a -- and enjoyed the status as a special unit. And I understood that the unit was deployed to the Trnovo theatre of war by the government of the Republic of Serbian Krajina as assistance at the prior invitation of the Supreme Command of Republika Srpska. Therefore, I understood that that was a unit of the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now read the following paragraph: "Witness Tomislav Kovac, in the relevant period, he was the deputy MUP minister of Republika Srpska, confirms in his statement the claims of Witness Milovanovic. He explained that the Skorpions units arrived in the Trnovo area as a unit of the Republic of Serbian Krajina from Erdut, which is well-known to him, because the arrival of any unit from any area could not have happened at that time without co-ordination with him." My question is this: Does this mean that the unit arrived in Trnovo and that for all of us, for the command structure, it was clear that it was a unit of the MUP of the Republic of Serbian Krajina? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, really, this opened an entirely new issue. It says up here that the special unit of the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina and its status was explained by Milan Milovanovic. It was sent by the government of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. In other words, if an army unit is -- an army unit, it cannot be sent anybody by the government. It could be done by the Ministry of Defence, perhaps. And if it was in co-ordination with our deputy minister of the interior, then one could arrive at a conclusion that that was a police unit. This is just a conclusion about how the unit arrived in the area, in whose co-ordination, in whose organisation, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Does every unit have a commander, as well as organs in charge of applying disciplinary measures for disciplinary breaches and crimes of different kinds?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on the rank of such a unit. If a unit is at a lower tactical level it has its commanders, "komandiri." It doesn't have any special organs. And even units up to a level of joint tactical groups which have commanders and organs in charge of special tasks do not have such organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In such a case, is a commander of such a unit responsible for every member of his unit and for all of the unit's activities? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A unit commander is the most responsible for the overall situation in his unit. By analogy, he is also responsible for the state of order in his unit, for the discipline of his soldiers, for any disciplinary breaches and crimes committed by his soldiers and similar things.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 65 ter 00008.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is a law. Actually, part of the Law on the Ministry of Interior of Republika Srpska. Here we see that the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska and Republika Srpska MUP received this document from the president of Republika Srpska, and that happened in 1995, on the 2nd of April, 1995. And it says here: "We were informed about some problems and confusion regarding the engagement of the MUP in combat activities, and the president hereby orders ..." And my question is this: Were you ever asked about this document when you testified in the Popovic case? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember whether any questions were put to me with regard to this document. However, I can -- I noted the date of the document, which is the 22nd of April, 1995. At the time, I was hospitalised. However, I don't see anything in dispute with regard to the fact that the Supreme Commander of the armed forces regulates relations between two very similar components, the police, on the one hand, and the army on the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: For the sake of the record, this document is already in evidence as P2419. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: General, sir, the military and the police, or, rather, the Ministry of Interior, were they duty-bound to comply with the orders of the Supreme Commander? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both the military and the police are duty-bound to comply with the Law on the Army, as well as the Law on the Internal Affairs. And also they are duty-bound to comply with the orders issued by the Supreme Commander, based on those two laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. This is precisely what it says here. Under 1 it says: "The Main Staff of the army shall hence-to-forth define more precisely and concretely their request for engagement an employment of MUP units in combat, in accordance with provisions of Article 14 of the Law on Application of the Law on Interior Affairs." My question is this: In that case, did -- was every command, including the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, duty-bound to define their requests for the engagement and employment of MUP units, be it MUP units of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, or --

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you repeat your question. Was the commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps duty bound -- I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, to which both the MUP of Republika Srpska and the Republic of Serbian Krajina units were attached, was it duty-bound to define the requests for the employment of those units that were attached to it for combat purposes.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I understand you. Based on this order, the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps was duty-bound to define its requests for engagement and employment of the units that arrived in its area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at the second bullet point where it says: "When MUP units are engaged in combat as part of the VRS troops, the Republika Srpska MUP shall precisely specify the responsibilities of the commanding officers and commanders when they resubordinate to the commander of the VRS unit in whose area of responsibility they are carrying out their combat tasks, pursuant to provisions of Article 14 ..." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us now, the commanding officers and commanders of units that arrived in the area of responsibility of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps pursuant to the order of the Supreme Command, were they duty-bound to define the roles of the commanding officers and commanders who were resubordinated to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this specific case, I don't know whether that was the case. However, starting with the military theory and the doctrine of command, and here I see that the Law on Internal Affairs is also quoted, I don't finds it logical to specify the obligations and duties of commanding officers and commanders when they are resubordinated. There's nothing special about it. He receives orders from the unit to which it is -- he is resubordinated and carries out that task in keeping with the rules of combat engagement. As members of the military police and you, as a security organ, had that problem, because rules do not envisage the employment of military units in combat. However, the situation demanded that that was done. So I can't tell you specifically whether those commanding officers and commanders of units resubordinated to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps had their obligations precisely defined. However, I believe that their obligations as commanding officers and commanders were regulated by some basic laws governing the work of the army and of the police. It is well-known what the duties of a commanding officer or a commander are, and they do not change once they are resubordinated to another unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now look at Article 13 of the Law on the Ministry of Interior where it says: "Police units shall participate in combat operations pursuant to the order of the supreme commander of the armed forces and the Ministry of the Interior." The second paragraph reads: "The minister of the interior commands police units of either staff of the command of the ministry police forces." My question is this: Is it the commander from the interior ministry who is in command of those units that are resubordinated to the army? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And now let's look at Article 14: "Police units having been engaged in combat activities by the order of the supreme commander of the armed force shall be subordinated to the commander of the unit in whose area of responsibility they are conducting out combat operations." My question is this: Were all units resubordinated to the corps command so that he would be able to carry out an operation in keeping with the decision and order that he had received from the superior commands?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Everybody has to be resubordinated to him. According to what I know, the Ministry of the Interior devised its own solution, according to which, if several units from different parts of the organisation are subordinated, for example, some of the special units from one centre and then from a special brigade in Bijeljina, then a staff is formed for the Ministry of Interior that is in charge of those units in a certain zone, and the commander of that staff is resubordinated to the commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, in this case, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And now let's look at paragraph 2, Article 14, where it says: "Police units are commanded by a MUP commander for the duration of the time when they are resubordinated to a unit of the Army of Republika Srpska. And while they're deployed, they cannot be scattered or divided." Is that correct? Just say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since this document has been admitted, as the President has said, there is no need to tendered it. I would like to call up D130. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let's quote the first paragraph, "Pursuant to the order of the deputy minister of the interior," and a number is quoted here. That's the first document we saw when we started talking about the resubordination. I was instructed to participate in the operation Srebrenica 1995 with some of the forces of the MUP: "The operation has been ongoing for five days already. The order specified that the combat group of the MUP in the aforementioned area shall be composed of the 2nd Special Detachment of Sekovici, the 1st Company from Zvornik, two companies of the joint forces of the MUP of the RSK, and a MUP company from the training centre on Jahorina. The group shall be formed on the 11th of July before 1200 hours. Of the aforementioned mentioned forces, the 2nd Special Detachment of the Sekovici police at the moment when the issue -- when the order was issued, was already engaged in combat in Srednje. The 1st Company, except for the special police units from Zvornik, was not mobilised. Both companies of the MUP RSK in combat in Trnovo and the company from the centre for training was at its base in Mount Jahorina." My question: Does this show that none of the police forces from Serbian Krajina Corps participated in combat in Srebrenica, or does it show something different? They had two companies in combat in Trnovo.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I read here, from what you have quoted from this document, I can only conclude that -- I don't know if this is a statement or a note by a commander, the commander of a combat group. In any case, we can see that -- that the operation in Srebrenica had been ongoing for five days, and that it was only then that he received his order to form a combat group. He received an order to form a combat group, and then he says that 2nd Detachment of the special police is engaged in combat in the Srednje sector which is north of Sarajevo on the other side towards Nisici. He also says that the 1st Company of the special unit of the police from Zvornik was not even mobilised. Those were police officers who worked in their public security stations. They were engaged in regular policing duties, and, as needed, they are mobilised and they form a company. The companies of the Republika Srpska Krajina MUP are in Trnovo, and a company from the training centre in Jahorina was there, on Jahorina. This shows us that it would have taken us some time for this combat group to be formed from all the specified units which were, at the time, in different areas and were mostly engaged in combat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, Mr. Tolimir. I have a question. Is there English translation available? In the list of your documents, there is no indication if there is a translation or not. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I am slightly taken aback, because when we were using this document, if I remember correctly, with Mr. Janc, there was a translation. Maybe it is a technical error or a combination of 65 ter documents from the Prosecution and from Defence. I am surprised myself there is no translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Indeed there is a translation. It would have to be loaded under 65 ter 87, and we'll find the identical document, same ERN number with the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It would be helpful to see that and we would like to see the first page to enable the witness to see what kind of document this is. Can we go to the first page in both languages, please. Then it's very -- can we go to the last page. How many pages are there? We can see an entry, 20th of July, 1995, and a signature which could be Ljubisa Borovcanin. Mr. Tolimir, do you want to put additional questions --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I kindly ask you to go back to this. I want to read the second paragraph, because I've already asked the question based on the first one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Or can I ask this: Can we see from this that units of the MUP were assembled and they were under the command of a certain officer from the ministry?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. From several MUP units, one combat group was formed, which was normal practice both in the army and in the police, and the Protection Regiment followed that pattern almost the entire duration of the war. That is to say, for a specific assignment, they would form a combat group from parts of various tactical units, and that's how they carried out assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It says I received the order at the forward command post in Trnovo, where I was commanding the joint forces of the MUP. During the night between the 10th and the 11th, I arrived at Jahorina where I met with the commander of the special police brigade and consulted him briefly about the method of engagement in Srebrenica: "Spaso Skoro, assistant commander of the Special Police Brigade, took over the command of the police forces in Trnovo." My question is: Is it the case that all joint forces, joint companies or other joint units had their own commands over their units, or they were resubordinated to corps units as envisaged by the Law on Internal Affairs?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every unit, regardless of how you engage it, how you use it, whether you are using a detachment of the special police just one, has its own commander, the detachment commander. If it's a company of the special police units, the company has its own company commander, and he commands the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Following that analogy, did the MUP of the Republic of Serbian Krajina have its own commander of various units beginning with squads to companies, because we know that there were two companies in Trnovo from the MUP of the Republic of Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no first-hand knowledge of this, but if we apply the same analogy and logic, that's the way it should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the Trial Chamber wishes to see this document, P1249, that's the Law on Internal Affairs under circumstances of immediate threat of war. This might be a useful document in reviewing and considering this exchange between the witness and myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I just have one suggestion to avoid a similar problem with other documents. We have the document in e-court already, both under 1D number and the 65 ter number of the Prosecution. In 65 ter 87, we should add D130, because D130 has a translation attached already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Whatever is the fact, I would like to ask the Registry to attach the translation of 65 ter 87 to D130. Then we have a complete document. It's already in evidence. Mr. Tolimir, it is your -- it is your cross-examination. You should decide how to proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I kindly ask that this suggestion made by my legal assistant be accepted. I agree with him on all matters so that I can move to the next document. I would like to see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please wait a moment. I already instructed the Registry to act according. The Registrar has the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Just for the record, the translation has been attached to Exhibit D130. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please carry on, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I kindly ask e-court to display P488.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We can see it's a document from the command of the 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade, 21st July, addressed to General Miletic, sent by Assistant Commander Major-General Zdravko Tolimir. In this document, I describe the situation in Zepa. Please look at and read item 4. That's what we'll be discussing. My question is: After reading this, do you see that I'm suggesting the use of chemicals, not weapons? As a commanding officer yourself, you can see the difference between chemicals and weapons.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have noticed this usage of chemical assets, or chemicals. In the terminology of security, I wouldn't say security of the police or the army, but chemical assets mean -- chemical means for temporary -- for disabling temporarily the enemy personnel; whereas, chemical weapon means something quite different. These are weapons for mass destruction of enemy personnel. And as far as I know, the Yugoslavia People's Army in the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia which was the predecessor of all the new states and armies, did not have chemical weapons in its possession.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know whether they had chemical assets, whether units had chemical assets; and, if so, what kind?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did have chemical assets. They were mostly in the possession of military police units, speaking of the army, and I know that police officers also had them. As for the army - and I'm talking mainly about the military police because I don't think other units had them - they had the following: Special hand-grenades; chemical rifles of the Shermolin [phoen] type; a back sprinkler, or sprayer; and launchers of chemical assets on the so-called combat armoured vehicles, BOVs. Those were the chemical assets. Mainly tear-gas, CS. CS are the initials of the inventor of this police asset, this particular agent. I believe I used it twice in the war. And both times, it was against Serbian forces in situations when I was forced to apply these to prevent some units from leaving their position without official leave. I don't think I need to specify which those units were. It doesn't matter to this trial. That's all I know about chemical agents or chemical assets.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now look at what it says next in this text. Am I suggesting the use of these chemical agents to break the enemy's defence in the areas of Stublic Radava and Brloska mountain?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, Brezova Ravan and Purtici.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since you mentioned RPGs, can we see document 65 ter 07393 in e-court. Since you explained its purpose and composition, you see now the manual. Was it the manual available to military police units which had these chemical agents?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If that's important, I could emphasise that I personally dealt with the testing of the training RPG chemical mine, M83.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let's look at page 27 of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir. If you are now going into details of this document, you should be aware of the time. It is 7.00. I agree you should continue with these kind of questions tomorrow. Only if it is one question, then you could try to conclude, but I think it's better to adjourn for the day.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I just wanted to ask one question after I show one paragraph. For instance, on that page, 27, because the witness explained all about the mine. He knows about it. He tested it. It says: "Use in combat against infiltrated groups." Do you see this? And I'll read that paragraph, 38. It's the use of RPG chemical skol mines. It says in combat against infiltrated enemy groups, RPG chemical training mines can successfully be used in searching the terrain in circling, in blocking infiltrated groups, and setting ambushes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The question is: Could these chemical training assets be used in both peacetime and in war, that you used yourself, and you know about them very well?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And you see in this rule or instruction you can see the full name of this asset, an RPG chemical training mine, which means that it is it filled with tear-gas, CS, nothing else. And it's certainly not a chemical weapon. Pay attention to the word "training" in the Serbian original. It sounds, skol; skol mine.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank the Trial Chamber for this small extension, and I thank everyone, the interpreters and everyone else. We will continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We must adjourn for the day. I have to remind you, sir, that you are not allowed to have contact about the content of your testimony during the break to either party. We adjourn and resume tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have to tell the parties that the Chamber is sitting tomorrow with two Judges because of the absence of Judge Mindua. He has another urgent appointment, and the next week, as I indicated yesterday, Judge Mindua and I, myself, are not able to be in court. Only Judge Nyambe would be able. This is not sufficient, as you know. Therefore, we had to cancel the hearings on Monday and Tuesday. The Chamber has decided to sit pursuant to Rule 15 bis tomorrow. We adjourn and resume at 9.00 in Courtroom II tomorrow.
